title: Feedback that lands: one piece of work, four moves
performance: before their next one-to-one, the viewer can raise a concern about one piece of a report's work as a short conversation: name the situation, describe the specific behaviour, say its impact, then ask for the report's view and agree a small, concrete next step, soon after the work and in a calm, private moment

audience.assumed_prior: manages at least one person; knows from both sides what giving and receiving feedback feels like, including a vague comment that left them unsure what to change; probably has no named method for it
audience.why: the brief's audience is new and mid-level people managers who already give feedback as part of the job (practitioners in the role) but are novices in this method; the knowledge sheet defines each move (F1 to F4, F6, F12, F13) and assumes nothing beyond office work
audience.motivation: probably assigned rather than chosen (not stated) and sceptical of training videos; what they care about is getting one piece of work fixed without a defensive conversation or a damaged working relationship, so relevance must land in the first seconds and nothing may sound like a lecture
audience.context: not stated in the brief; plan for a desk or laptop with sound and captions on (the project requests captions), first-language English assumed but not confirmed, so screens carry short anchors and nothing rests on audio alone

strategy.name: scenario_led
strategy.rationale: the knowledge sheet gives a sequence of conversational moves (F1, F2 to F4, F6, F12, F13) plus one sharp distinction, describing the work versus judging the person (F5), and warns that the structure is not a script (F15); that is a judgement skill used live in a conversation, and the brief asks for one invented moment played wrong and then replayed, so the lesson teaches best by stopping Maya's conversation at each decision point and showing what the report does with each line
strategy.signature_move: play Maya's tempting line, show what the report does with it, replay that moment with the move, THEN name the move

misconceptions.belief: a short, honest verdict like 'that update wasn't great' is direct feedback, and the person will know what to fix
misconceptions.why_tempting: it feels direct and quick, it is true as far as it goes, and it spares both people an awkward conversation
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge F9 (a vague verdict gives nothing specific to act on and is heard as a judgement), F4
misconceptions.refutation: state it fairly in the presenter's voice (it sounds like honesty), then show the report's thought aside: they cannot tell what to change, they hear it as being about them, and their reply is a defence; the update itself sits untouched on screen, nothing in it has changed

misconceptions.belief: it is fine to save a concern up for the next review, or to drop it in passing when it comes to mind
misconceptions.why_tempting: saving it up postpones a difficult conversation, and a passing remark feels lighter and less formal
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge F10 (soon, while both remember it, at a calm private moment, not in passing), F11 (one piece of work)
misconceptions.refutation: sec1 shows the cost (days later, in a corridor, the report barely remembers the update); sec3 replays the same concern the same afternoon, in a quiet room, about that one update only, and the report can picture the moment straight away; per F10's caveat, soon means while it is fresh, not instantly

misconceptions.belief: calling it what it is, 'careless' or 'sloppy', is being specific
misconceptions.why_tempting: a label feels precise and honest, and it names what the manager is actually worried about
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge F5 (describing behaviour versus judging the person), F4 (observable behaviour), F9
misconceptions.refutation: at the behaviour move, Maya's thought aside drafts 'you were careless with it'; it fades and is replaced by 'the update didn't say when the change takes effect'; the first names a person and gives them nothing to fix, the second names something in the work anyone could have seen and that can be fixed (slowdown 1)

misconceptions.belief: once you have said your piece, the feedback is done; asking for their view just invites an argument
misconceptions.why_tempting: the manager has done the hard part, and a question feels like reopening it or losing control of the conversation
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge F2 (ask, then agree a next step, so it is a conversation, not a verdict), F12 (they add context the manager may not have), F13 (a small, concrete next step)
misconceptions.refutation: the pause_predict puts Maya's tempting close ('so, just be more careful next time') on screen; the reveal shows her ask instead, the report adds context she did not have, and the next step they agree is one they chose together; per F12's caveat, the question has to be a real one

running_example.framing: clearly invented, introduced with 'say' in the first line of sec1; an ordinary office, no real company, no industry jargon, no drama, no raised voices
cast: Maya, the manager (illustrated woman in her 30s, office clothes); she gets it wrong first
her report, unnamed, a simpler code-drawn figure or seen from behind
the presenter at the opening and the close only, never inside the scenario, never named
running_example.piece_of_work: a client update that went out unclear: it did not say when the change takes effect (the knowledge sheet's own illustrative example, F5)
invented_details: impact: say, the client wrote back to ask when the change starts, and the answer took another day
context the report adds when asked: say, the date was still being confirmed when the update went out
agreed next step: when a date is not confirmed, the update says so and says when it will be; Maya looks at the next update with them on Thursday
running_example.rule: these are the ONLY invented details; one piece of work throughout, no second example, no HR or formal process, no statistics

hook.sketch: You have probably said it, or heard it: 'that update wasn't great.' So what, exactly, was the other person supposed to fix?
hook.on_screen_essence: 'That wasn't great.' So what do they fix?

arc.promise: by the end you have four moves you can use in your next one-to-one, so one piece of work gets fixed, not defended
arc.bridge_from_prior: sec1 opens from the vague comment the viewer has given or received, and from the instinct that saying it plainly is the honest thing to do

sections.title: The verdict that gets defended
sections.goal: the viewer can explain why a vague verdict about one piece of work, said days later and in passing, gets defended against instead of acted on
sections.carrier: scenario: Maya walks past her report's desk days after the client update went out (a calendar strip behind them shows the days that have passed) and says her vague line; the report's thought aside fills with defences ('it was fine', 'nobody said anything', 'what does she mean?') while the update itself stays on screen with nothing in it changed
sections.recap: vague, late, in passing, and heard as being about them
sections.teaching_notes: open with 'say' to frame the scene as invented; Maya gets it wrong first, plainly, with no villain music; refute misconception 1 here; the narrator names the two costs from F9 once each (nothing specific to act on, heard as a judgement of them) and adds F9's caveat in a few words (some people take it well, it is a tendency); F7 and F8 inform why this matters but are NOT voiced

sections.title: Four moves, as a common practice
sections.goal: the viewer can summarise the four moves in order: the situation, the specific behaviour, its impact, then ask for their view and agree a next step
concepts: ask and agree a next step
sections.carrier: checklist: a short four-line card builds once, one line per move, each line appearing as it is spoken with a short plain gloss (when and where; what they did or said; what it caused; your view, then next step); the card then shrinks to a corner, where it stays for sec3
sections.teaching_notes: introduce the moves as 'a common practice' that many organisations teach, never as research and never naming any organisation (approver decision); say once that it is a habit, not a script, and should sound like you (F15, F16); exactly four new terms, so nothing else is introduced here; keep it brisk, these viewers notice padding

sections.title: The same update, replayed
sections.goal: the viewer can use the first three moves on one piece of work: name the situation, describe the behaviour instead of judging the person, and state what it caused
sections.carrier: scenario replay: the same concern, now the same afternoon in a quiet small meeting room; the four-move card in the corner ticks each line as Maya says it; at the behaviour move her thought aside drafts 'you were careless with it', which fades and is rewritten as 'the update didn't say when the change takes effect'; the report's posture eases from braced to listening as each move lands
sections.teaching_notes: worked example of moves one to three, every move narrated with the signature move (tempting line, what the report does with it, replay, name the move); Maya says the moves in her own words, not off a form (F15); refute misconceptions 2 and 3; this is slowdown 1 (describe the work, not the person); the replay stops BEFORE move four: Maya's thought aside drafts her tempting close, which becomes the pause_predict; this fades the brief's full replay into a completion problem on purpose, so the viewer does the last move first

sections.title: Ask, agree, then your own week
sections.goal: the viewer can carry out all four moves on one piece of their own work, ending with a real question and a small, concrete next step
sections.carrier: dialogue then worksheet: the reveal scene shows Maya ask instead of closing, the report adds the context she did not have, and the agreed next step appears as a small note with a day on it (Thursday); then the screen goes light and warm: the four-move card returns blank, for a piece of the viewer's own work, one line filling at a time as the narrator gives one short prompt per move
sections.teaching_notes: the reveal answers the pause_predict and refutes misconception 4; this is slowdown 2 (the ask: a real question before the next step); then the valley: warmer and slower, speaking to the viewer about their own week; independent practice: the viewer picks one piece of a report's work from this week and walks the four moves in their head, with a beat after each prompt (no stopping check); one line only on F14 (the same moves work for something that went well); F12's caveat in a few words: the question has to be a real one

arc.payoff: The presenter returns to the opening line, 'that update wasn't great', now as one specific thing, said soon, ending in a question, and hands the viewer their next one-to-one.

practice_ladder.what: Maya's replayed conversation runs moves one to three with every move narrated and marked on the card; kept brisk for practitioners (expertise reversal), but fully shown because the method is new to them
the replay stops before move four; the viewer sees Maya's tempting close and predicts which move should replace it before she shows it
the viewer walks all four moves against one piece of a report's work from their own week, with one prompt and a beat per move

slowdown_at: describe the work, not the person: 'careless' rewritten as what the update did not say (sec3)
the ask: a real question before the next step (sec4)

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Keep the report's last thought in mind: 'what does she mean?' The rest of this is how to make sure nobody has to ask that.
Maya has said the situation, the behaviour and the impact. Now she's about to close with 'So, just be more careful next time.' Which move should replace that line? Pause and decide before she does.
recall_moments.fork: the viewer chooses between treating 'be more careful' as the next step (tempting) and the fourth move, ask for their view and then agree a small, concrete next step
recall_moments.answer: the fourth move: ask for the report's view first, then agree a small, concrete next step together
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: 'be more careful' already is the next step: it is not; it is a verdict about the person, it names no piece of work and no day, and nobody asked the report anything, so it gives them nothing they helped choose (F2, F12, F13)

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Before the card comes back: say the four moves to yourself. Situation. Behaviour. Impact. Ask, then agree.

transfer_tasks: before your next one-to-one, pick one piece of a report's work from this week and note one line for each move: when and where, what they did, what it caused, and the question you will ask
the next time you hear yourself about to say a verdict ('that wasn't great', 'be more careful'), swap it for what they did and what it caused
use the same moves on something that went well: name the behaviour and its impact, so they know exactly what to keep doing
pocket_rule: One specific thing, said soon, ending in a question.

persona.voice: a colleague who has had these conversations and got some of them wrong: plain, direct, a little dry; never teacher-like, never cheerleading; talks to the viewer as a peer (from the brief's voice note; no persona is set yet)
persona.delivery_notes: say each point once and move on; level and matter-of-fact in sec1, no dramatic voice when Maya gets it wrong; brisk on the four-move card; say Maya's lines the way a real manager would say them, slightly hesitant at the rewrite; slow down and drop the pitch on the two slowdowns only; read the pause_predict prompt plainly and stop; warmer and slower in sec4, speaking to the viewer about their own week; dry and short on recaps

narration_contract: address every enumerated point on screen in order (the four moves, the three defences in the thought aside, the four lines of the blank card); never recite on-screen text word for word; frame Maya's scene as invented once with 'say' and keep the client update the only example; present the four moves as a common practice throughout, never as research, and never name any organisation as its origin; do not voice F7 or F8, they inform the plan's reasoning only; no statistics, percentages, ratios, studies or quotes (knowledge sheet not_claimed); never tell the viewer they have been doing it wrong

approver_decisions.origin_naming: do not name the organisation behind the situation, behaviour, impact structure; say 'a common practice' (F1 caveat, requester decision 2026-10-02)
approver_decisions.research_findings: F7 and F8 may inform the reasoning (why describe the task, not the person) but are not voiced; the spoken lesson stays practical (requester decision 2026-10-02)
approver_decisions.report_name: the report stays unnamed (brief open question; not decided otherwise)

gagne.attention: hook: 'that update wasn't great', so what do they fix?
gagne.objective: promise: four moves for your next one-to-one so one piece of work gets fixed, not defended
gagne.recall_prior: sec1 bridges from the vague comment the viewer has given or received
gagne.present: sec1 to sec4 in the order each idea becomes usable: why the verdict fails, the four moves, moves one to three worked, move four and own work
gagne.guidance: signature move (tempting line, what the report does with it, replay, name the move) at each decision point; worked replay in sec3
gagne.practice: pause_predict after sec3 (faded move four); own-week walk in sec4
gagne.feedback: the reveal in sec4 shows the ask and explains why 'be more careful' is a verdict, not a next step
gagne.assess: pause_predict after sec3 can be got wrong; recall_prompt after sec4 has the viewer say the four moves before the card returns
gagne.transfer: sec4 own-week walk; three transfer tasks; pocket rule; payoff hands over the next one-to-one

merrill.problem_centered: Maya's one unclear client update IS the running problem, from hook to payoff
merrill.activation: sec1 bridges from the viewer's own experience of a vague comment
merrill.demonstration: sec3 replays the conversation and shows each move landing before naming it
merrill.application: the pause_predict makes the viewer choose move four; sec4 has them walk all four on their own work
merrill.integration: sec4 own-week walk, transfer tasks for the next one-to-one, and the positive-feedback use (F14)

mayer.coherence: one invented piece of work with three invented details; no second example, no HR process, no research claims on screen
mayer.signalling: two slowdowns only: describe the work not the person (sec3), the real question (sec4); the four-move card ticks as each move lands
mayer.redundancy: screens carry the card, short glosses, Maya's drafted lines and the report's thought aside; narration explains; the pause_predict question is the one full sentence on screen, readable in the pause
mayer.contiguity: each card line appears as it is spoken; each tick lands as Maya says the move; the rewrite replaces 'careless' as the narrator names the difference
mayer.segmenting: four short sections, one step each; sec2 introduces exactly the four move names and nothing else
mayer.pre_training: sec2 names the four moves before sec3 runs them in the conversation

arcs.attention: the vague line every manager recognises; carrier variety (scenario, checklist, scenario replay, dialogue then worksheet) and energy (build, steady, peak, rest)
arcs.relevance: in the first seconds: getting one piece of work fixed without a defensive conversation (brief cares_about); no lecture, colleague voice
arcs.confidence: the moves are shown worked before the viewer is asked anything; the pause_predict asks about a move they have already seen on the card
arcs.satisfaction: the viewer names move four before Maya does, walks it on their own work, and the payoff returns to the opening line, now fixed
